claim: Exosomes isolated from patient-derived prostate CAFs have a size distribution from 30 to 100 nm.
source: The particle size analysis of isolated exosomes showed particles with size distribution from 30 to 100 nm (Figure 1A), which is consistent with previous observations (Xiao et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by particle size analysis data shown in Figure 1A and is consistent with cited literature (Xiao et al., 2014).

claim: CAF-derived exosomes express CD63, a surface antigen marker.
source: We confirmed exosomes' expression of CD63, a surface antigen marker, through flow analysis of Dynabeads conjugated with anti-CD63 antibody (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating CD63 expression on exosomes.

claim: CAF-derived exosomes are taken up by prostate cancer cells (PC3).
source: As indicated by shift in the peaks, CDEs are indeed taken up by cancer cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing peak shifts in Figure 1C and fluorescence microscopy in Figure 1D.

claim: 200 μg/ml of CDEs was used as the working concentration in subsequent experiments.
source: Hence, in subsequent experiments we used 200 μg/ml of CDEs as the working concentration (Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2012 and saturation curve data in Figure 1E.

claim: CDEs enhance proliferation of PC3 cells with increasing exosome concentration.
source: CDEs enhanced proliferation of PC3 cells with increasing exosomes concentration (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Basal oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) was significantly inhibited with increasing concentration of CDEs added to PC3 cells.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that basal oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS, indicated by OCR) was significantly inhibited with increasing concentration of CDEs added to PC3 cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by oxygen consumption rate measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Exosomes from control conditions (PC3 cells, IMR-90 fibroblasts, and blank media) were ineffective in modulating cancer cells' OCR.
source: As seen in the figure, exosomes from control conditions were ineffective in modulating cancer cells' OCR.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing no OCR changes with control exosomes.

claim: Exogenous addition of CDEs reduced OCR in all prostate cancer cell lines tested (PC3, DU145, 22RV1 and E006AA).
source: Remarkably, exogenous addition of CDEs reduced OCR in all prostate cancer cell lines.
evidence: The claim is supported by OCR measurements across four prostate cancer cell lines shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cytochalasin D (CytoD) partially rescued the reduction of OCR in PC3 cells caused by CDEs.
source: Notably, CytoD could partially rescue this reduction of OCR in PC3 cells, thus confirming the CAF exosomes mediated reduction of OCR in cancer cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by OCR measurements with CytoD treatment shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CytoD inhibits exosome uptake in various cell systems.
source: CytoD has been shown to inhibit exosome uptake in various cell systems (Casella et al., 1981; Feng et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Casella et al., 1981 and Feng et al., 2010.

claim: Both maximal and reserve mitochondrial capacity of cancer cells were significantly reduced in presence of CDEs.
source: Both maximal and reserve mitochondrial capacity of cancer cells were significantly reduced in presence of CDEs (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by mitochondrial capacity measurements using FCCP and antimycin shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Exogenous addition of CDEs significantly reduced mitochondrial membrane potential within cancer cells.
source: As seen in Figure 2F, exogenous addition of CDEs significantly reduced mitochondrial membrane potential within cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by mitochondrial membrane potential measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Transcript levels for OXPHOS related ATP synthase complex genes were downregulated in cells cultured with CDEs.
source: Microarray data revealed that transcript levels for OXPHOS related ATP synthase complex genes were downregulated in cells cultured with CDEs.
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray analysis and GSEA showing negative enrichment for OXPHOS genes in Figure 2G.

claim: Both cytochrome B (CYTB) and cytochrome C oxidase I (COXI) have lower transcript expression levels when PC3 cells were cultured with exogenous CDEs.
source: Furthermore, we found that both cytochrome B (CYTB) and cytochrome C oxidase I (COXI), which are components of Complexes III and IV of the electron transport chain, respectively, have lower transcript expression levels when PC3 cells were cultured with exogenous CDEs (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by q-PCR data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The relative abundance of miRNAs that target oxidative phosphorylation genes is higher in exosomes than most other miRNA.
source: The relative abundance of miRNAs that target oxidative phosphorylation genes is higher in exosomes than most other miRNA as seen in the density distribution plot (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by NanoString miRNA measurements shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The top 30 most abundant miRNAs across the exosomes sampled target one or more OXPHOS genes.
source: The top 30 most abundant miRNAs across the exosomes sampled, target one or more OXPHOS genes, which is validated by measuring the decrease in mRNA levels of these genes after treatment with exosomes (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by NanoString miRNA data and mRNA measurements shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Co-transfection of mir-22, let7a and mir-125b in PC3 cells results in a decrease in OCR.
source: In line with our hypothesis, we see a decrease in OCR in PC3 cells co-transfected with miRNAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by OCR measurements after miRNA transfection shown in Figure 2K.

claim: CDEs significantly increased glycolysis in cancer cells when compared to cancer cells cultured without exosomes.
source: As seen in the figure, these exosomes significantly increased glycolysis in cancer cells when compared to cancer cells cultured without exosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by ECAR measurements across four prostate cancer cell lines shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CytoD partially inhibited the increase of ECAR caused by CDEs.
source: Notably, CytoD partially inhibited this increase of ECAR, thus confirming the role of exosomes in increase of glycolysis in cancer cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ECAR measurements with CytoD treatment shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CDEs increased glucose uptake and lactate secretion when compared to cancer cells cultured without exogenously added exosomes.
source: Consistent with above results, CDEs increased glucose uptake and lactate secretion when compared to cancer cells cultured without exogenously added exosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by glucose uptake and lactate secretion measurements shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: CDEs increased the lactate levels in the cancer cells.
source: We found that the CDEs increased the lactate levels in the cancer cells (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by 13C-labeled glucose tracer analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The percentage of M3 pyruvate and M3 lactate was increased due to CDEs.
source: Further, the percentage of M3 pyruvate and M3 lactate was increased due to CDEs; however, there is a corresponding decrease in the percentage of M2 citrate and M3 citrate (Figure 3G-I).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass isotopologue distribution data from 13C-glucose tracing shown in Figures 3G-I.

claim: The percentage of M2 citrate, M2 α-ketoglutarate, M2 fumarate, M2 malate, and M2 glutamate was significantly reduced in cancer cells in presence of CDEs.
source: Consistent with the decreased OXPHOS observed in cancer cells due to CDEs, the percentage of M2 citrate, M2 α-ketoglutarate, M2 fumarate, M2 malate, and M2 glutamate was also significantly reduced in cancer cells in presence of CDEs (Figure 3I–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass isotopologue distribution data from 13C-glucose tracing shown in Figures 3I-M.

claim: The percentage of 13C α-ketoglutarate from 13C labeled glucose was significantly reduced in presence of CDEs.
source: In line with our observations, the percentage of 13C α-ketoglutarate from 13C labeled glucose was significantly reduced (Figure 3N).
evidence: The claim is supported by isotope tracing data showing reduced glucose contribution to α-ketoglutarate in Figure 3N.

claim: Addition of CDEs increased M5 glutamate and M5 α-ketoglutarate in cancer cells.
source: Our MID data reveals that addition of CDEs increased M5 glutamate and M5 α-ketoglutarate in cancer cells thereby indicating that exosomes enhance glutamine's entry into TCA cycle (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass isotopologue distribution data from 13C-glutamine tracing shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: There was significant increase in M5 citrate, M3 fumarate and M3 malate in cancer cells in the presence of exogenously added exosomes.
source: Notably, there was significant increase in M5 citrate, M3 fumarate and M3 malate in cancer cells in the presence of exogenously added exosomes thus suggesting that cancer cells rely critically on reductive glutamine metabolism when normal mitochondrial function is disrupted by stromal microenvironment (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass isotopologue distribution data from 13C-glutamine tracing shown in Figures 4D-F.

claim: Exosomes increased the ratio of α-ketoglutarate to citrate abundance in cancer cells significantly.
source: To obtain mechanistic understanding of CDEs induced increased reductive carboxylation in cancer cells; we measured the ratio of α-ketoglutarate to citrate abundance in cancer cells and found that exosomes increased this ratio significantly (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolite abundance ratio measurements shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The increased ratio of α-ketoglutarate to citrate was recently shown to promote reductive glutamine metabolism.
source: The increased ratio of α-ketoglutarate to citrate was recently shown to promote reductive glutamine metabolism and it correlated with reductive glutamine's contribution to citrate (Fendt et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fendt et al., 2013.

claim: The ratio of M4/M5 citrate confirmed that there is a significant increase in glutamine's reductive metabolism in presence of exosomes.
source: Consistent with previous reports, the ratio of M4/M5 citrate, which represents the ratio of glutamine to citrate through oxidative metabolism over reductive metabolism, confirmed our above results that there is a significant increase in glutamine's reductive metabolism in presence of exosomes (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by isotopologue ratio analysis shown in Figures 4H-I.

claim: Exosomes decreased glucose contribution to palmitate.
source: Similar to our earlier observation that CDEs reduced glucose contribution to TCA cycle metabolites in cancer cells, we found that exosomes also decreased glucose contribution to palmitate. This is evident from the shift in high mass isotopologues of palmitate to lower mass isotopologues derived from U-13C6 glucose, when cells are cultured with exosomes (Figure 4J).
evidence: The claim is supported by 13C-glucose tracing to palmitate shown in Figure 4J.

claim: There is a shift from low to high mass palmitate isotopologues derived from U-13C5 glutamine in presence of CDEs.
source: Conversely, there is a shift in the reverse direction, i.e. from low to high mass palmitate isotopologues derived from U-13C5 glutamine, in presence of CDEs (Figure 4K).
evidence: The claim is supported by 13C-glutamine tracing to palmitate shown in Figure 4K.

claim: ISA indicated a significant decrease in the fraction of glucose contribution to lipogenic acetyl-CoA in cancer cells cultured with exosomes.
source: In line with above results, ISA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) indicated a significant decrease in the fraction of glucose contribution to lipogenic acetyl-CoA in cancer cells cultured with exosomes (Figure 4L).
evidence: The claim is supported by isotopologue spectral analysis shown in Figure 4L.

claim: There is a two-fold increase in glutamine's contribution to lipogenic acetyl-CoA via the reductive carboxylation pathway in presence of CDEs.
source: More importantly, there is a two-fold increase in glutamine's contribution to lipogenic acetyl-CoA via the reductive carboxylation pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by isotopologue spectral analysis shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Acetate concentrations were detected in cancer cell media at significant levels.
source: Indeed, acetate concentrations were detected in our cancer cell media at significant levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by acetate measurements in media shown in Figure 4M.

claim: CDEs increased acetate contribution to lipids.
source: Interestingly, we noticed from the shift in palmitate mass isotopologues that CDEs increased acetate contribution to lipids (Figure 4N) but decreased the pyruvate contribution (Figure 4O).
evidence: The claim is supported by 13C-acetate tracing to palmitate shown in Figure 4N.

claim: CDEs decreased pyruvate contribution to lipids.
source: Interestingly, we noticed from the shift in palmitate mass isotopologues that CDEs increased acetate contribution to lipids (Figure 4N) but decreased the pyruvate contribution (Figure 4O).
evidence: The claim is supported by 13C-pyruvate tracing to palmitate shown in Figure 4O.

claim: Cancer cells cultured with CDEs showed an increase in acetate's contribution with a concomitant decrease in pyruvate's contribution to palmitate production.
source: ISA results confirm these observations, where cancer cells cultured with CDEs showed an increase in acetate's contribution with a concomitant decrease in pyruvate's contribution to palmitate production (Figure 4P).
evidence: The claim is supported by isotopologue spectral analysis shown in Figure 4P.

claim: High amounts of lactate and acetate were found in both prostate and pancreatic CDEs.
source: Notably, we found high amounts of lactate and acetate in both prostate and pancreatic CDEs (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzymatic assay measurements of intra-exosomal lactate and acetate shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: High concentrations of citrate and pyruvate along with significant presence of α-ketoglutarate, fumarate and malate were found in exosomes.
source: Further, to prove these hypotheses we performed GC-MS analysis for intra-exosomal metabolites and found high concentrations of citrate and pyruvate along with significant presence of α-ketoglutarate, fumarate and malate (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GC-MS measurements of intra-exosomal TCA cycle metabolites shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Markedly high levels of glutamine, arginine, glutamate, proline, alanine, threonine, serine, asparagine, valine, and leucine were found in prostate CAF exosomes.
source: To further expand our findings, we performed ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC), and found markedly high levels of glutamine, arginine, glutamate, proline, alanine, threonine, serine, asparagine, valine, and leucine in prostate CAF exosomes (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by UPLC measurements of intra-exosomal amino acids shown in Figure 5D.

claim: High levels of glutamine, threonine, phenylalanine, valine, isoleucine, glycine, arginine, and serine were found in pancreatic CDEs.
source: Additionally, in pancreatic CDEs, we found high levels of glutamine, threonine, phenylalanine, valine, isoleucine, glycine, arginine, and serine (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by UPLC measurements of intra-exosomal amino acids shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Intact stearate and palmitate were found at high levels in both prostate and pancreatic CDEs.
source: Remarkably, through GC-MS analysis of intra-exosomal lipids, we found intact stearate (Figure 5F) and palmitate (Figure 5G) at high levels in both prostate and pancreatic CDEs.
evidence: The claim is supported by GC-MS measurements of intra-exosomal lipids shown in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: Exosomes harbor an 'off-the-shelf' pool of metabolite cargo, TCA cycle metabolites, amino acids, and lipids.
source: Our results offer definitive proof for the first time that exosomes harbor an 'off-the-shelf' pool of metabolite cargo, TCA cycle metabolites, amino acids, and lipids, which can fuel the metabolic activity of the recipient cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive intra-exosomal metabolomics data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Exosomes can supply metabolites to cancer cells under both complete and nutrient deprivation conditions.
source: Notably, our results substantiate that exosomes can supply metabolites to cancer cells under both complete and nutrient deprivation conditions (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by 13C-labeled exosome tracing experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is a significant increase in the contribution of CDEs to cancer cells' metabolites pools in nutrient deprived conditions, as compared to complete medium cultures.
source: However, and in concordance with hypothesis, we found that there is a significant increase in the contribution of CDEs to cancer cells' metabolites pools in nutrient deprived conditions, as compared to complete medium cultures.
evidence: The claim is supported by 13C-labeled exosome tracing experiments comparing complete and deprivation conditions shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Substantial labeling of intracellular amino acids in cancer cells was detected, including M5 glutamine, M6 lysine, and M6 leucine from labeled CDEs.
source: We detected substantial labeling of intracellular amino acids in cancer cells, which included M5 glutamine, M6 lysine, and M6 leucine.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass isotopologue distribution data from 13C-labeled exosome experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Labeled TCA cycle metabolites from labeled 13C-glutamine supplied by CDEs were detected in cancer cells.
source: We also detected M5 glutamate derived from mitochondrial glutaminolysis and labeled TCA cycle metabolites from labeled 13C-glutamine supplied by CDEs (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass isotopologue distribution data from 13C-labeled exosome experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Exosomes account for approximately 16% of phenylalanine, 14% of glutamine, 12% of lysine and 5% of leucine pools in PC3 cells.
source: We observed that exosomes account for approximately 16% of phenylalanine, 14% of glutamine, 12% of lysine and 5% of leucine pools in PC3 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by mean enrichment calculations from 13C-labeled exosome experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CDEs were able to rescue reduction of proliferation under nutrient deprivation conditions.
source: CDEs were able to rescue reduction of proliferation under nutrient deprivation conditions (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data under nutrient deprivation shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The rescue effect of CDEs on proliferation is reduced by adding CytoD, heparin and lysosomal degradation inhibitor chloroquine.
source: However, this rescue effect is reduced to varying extents by adding CytoD, heparin and lysosomal degradation inhibitor choloroquine (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data with inhibitors shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Addition of macropinocytosis inhibitor EIPA counters the rescue of CDEs under deprivation.
source: Similarly, addition of macropinocytosis inhibitor EIPA also counters the rescue of CDEs under deprivation (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data with EIPA treatment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: CDEs could rescue loss of proliferation in both BxPC3 and MiaPaCa-2 pancreatic cancer cell lines.
source: Notably, CDEs could rescue loss of proliferation in both cancer cell lines, thereby suggesting that internalization or uptake and supply of exosomes derived metabolites in cancer cells is Kras independent.
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data in wild-type and activated Kras expressing pancreatic cancer cells shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Internalization or uptake and supply of exosomes derived metabolites in cancer cells is Kras independent.
source: Notably, CDEs could rescue loss of proliferation in both cancer cell lines, thereby suggesting that internalization or uptake and supply of exosomes derived metabolites in cancer cells is Kras independent.
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data comparing wild-type Kras (BxPC3) and activated Kras (MiaPaCa-2) cells shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Heparin inhibited the rescue of proliferation by CDEs in pancreatic cancer cell lines under nutrient deprived conditions.
source: Furthermore, this rescue of proliferation by CDEs in pancreatic cancer cell lines was inhibited by receptor mediated endocytosis inhibitor heparin (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data with heparin treatment shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: iKras-1 cells with or without doxycycline showed similar proliferation increases with CDEs.
source: As shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2, iKras-1 cells with or without doxycycline showed similar proliferation increases with CDEs, thereby suggesting that internalization or uptake and supply of exosome-derived metabolites in cancer cells is Kras independent.
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data using doxycycline inducible Kras-G12D cell line shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: OCR of both BxPC3 and MiaPaCa-2 cells were decreased in presence of pancreatic CDEs.
source: In line with results obtained in prostate cancer cells, we found that OCR of both BxPC3 and MiaPaCa-2 cells were decreased in presence of pancreatic CDEs (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by OCR measurements in pancreatic cancer cells shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Both maximal and reserve mitochondrial capacity of pancreatic cancer cells were significantly reduced in presence of pancreatic CDEs.
source: Both maximal and reserve mitochondrial capacity of pancreatic cancer cells were significantly reduced in presence of pancreatic CDEs further confirming mitochondrial respiratory capacity inhibition in cancer cells by CAF exosomes (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by mitochondrial capacity measurements shown in Figure 7D.

claim: There was a corresponding increase in ECAR in both pancreatic cancer cell lines in presence of CDEs.
source: Furthermore, there was a corresponding increase in ECAR in both pancreatic cancer cell lines in presence of CDEs (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ECAR measurements in pancreatic cancer cells shown in Figure 7E.

claim: CDEs increased lactate levels in pancreatic cancer cells using U-13C6 glucose labeling based isotope tracer analysis.
source: This was corroborated by increased lactate levels in the cancer cells in presence of exosomes using U-13C6 glucose labeling based isotope tracer analysis of pancreatic cancer cells in presence of CAF exosomes (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by 13C-glucose tracing data in pancreatic cancer cells shown in Figure 7F.

claim: CDEs decreased percentage contribution of glucose to α-ketoglutarate in both pancreatic cancer cell lines.
source: Concomitantly, CDEs decreased percentage contribution of glucose to α-ketoglutarate in both pancreatic cancer cell lines (Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by 13C-glucose tracing data in pancreatic cancer cells shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Exosomes from pancreatic CAFs significantly increased the reductive glutamine metabolism in both wild-type and activated Kras expressing pancreatic cancer cells.
source: In line with the results obtained in prostate cancers, we found that exosomes from pancreatic CAFs significantly increased the reductive glutamine metabolism (Figure 7H–J, Figure 7—figure supplement 4). Remarkably, this CAF exosomes-mediated increase of reductive glutamine metabolism was detected in both wild-type and activated Kras expressing pancreatic cancer cells, thus suggesting that metabolic reprogramming induced by stromal exosomes in cancer cells is not only Kras independent but is broadly observed in many cancers.
evidence: The claim is supported by 13C-glutamine tracing data in both BxPC3 and MiaPaCa-2 cells shown in Figures 7H-J.

claim: Metabolic reprogramming induced by stromal exosomes in cancer cells is Kras independent.
source: Remarkably, this CAF exosomes-mediated increase of reductive glutamine metabolism was detected in both wild-type and activated Kras expressing pancreatic cancer cells, thus suggesting that metabolic reprogramming induced by stromal exosomes in cancer cells is not only Kras independent but is broadly observed in many cancers.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative data in wild-type and activated Kras expressing cells shown in Figure 7.

claim: CAFs comprise the majority of cell types within the TME.
source: CAFs comprise the majority of cell types within the TME, and their reciprocal interactions with cancer cells have been well documented (Whiteside, 2008; Hazlehurst et al., 2003; Karnoub et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Whiteside, 2008; Hazlehurst et al., 2003; Karnoub et al., 2007.

claim: CDEs enhance drug resistance in colorectal cancer stem cells by regulating the Wnt pathway.
source: Recently, Hu et al. have discovered that CDEs enhance drug resistance in colorectal cancer stem cells by regulating the Wnt pathway and this effect can be reversed by inhibiting exosome secretion (Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hu et al., 2015.

claim: Exosomes range between 30–100 nm in diameter and have a bilayered membrane.
source: Exosomes range between 30–100 nm in diameter, have a bilayered membrane (Johnstone et al., 1987) and express surface marker such as CD63 (Christianson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Johnstone et al., 1987 and Christianson et al., 2013.

claim: Exosomes contain proteins, nucleic acids and miRNAs.
source: Recent studies indicate that they contain proteins, nucleic acids and miRNAs (Ekström et al., 2012; Costa-Silva et al., 2015; Simons and Raposo, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ekström et al., 2012; Costa-Silva et al., 2015; Simons and Raposo, 2009.

claim: CAFs can induce metabolic reprogramming in cancer cells.
source: Although it has been shown that CAFs can induce metabolic reprogramming in cancer cells (Brauer et al., 2013), the contribution of CDEs in this phenomenon, if any, has not been elucidated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Brauer et al., 2013.

claim: Macropinocytosis of circulating proteins could supply amino acids to nutrient-deprived cancer cells.
source: Recent studies have shown that macropinocytosis of circulating proteins (especially albumin) could supply amino acids to nutrient-deprived cancer cells (Commisso et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Commisso et al., 2013.

claim: Synthetic liposomes did not alter cell proliferation, OCR and ECAR in both prostate and pancreatic cancer cells.
source: Our data suggests that liposomes did not alter cell proliferation, OCR and ECAR in both prostate (PC3) and pancreatic cancer cells (MiaPaCa-2 and BxPC3) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments with synthetic liposomes shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The working concentration of 200 μg/ml corresponded to ratio between 1 and 5 CAFs per cancer cell.
source: A concentration of 200 μg/ml corresponded to ratio between 1 and 5 CAFs per cancer cell and hence, is within the range reported in the literature.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from exosome yield and comparison to literature ratios.

claim: CDEs create hypoxia mimicking environment in cancer cells leading to an increase in reductive carboxylation of glutamine.
source: This suggests that CDEs create hypoxia mimicking environment in cancer cells leading to an increase in reductive carboxylation of glutamine in cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CDEs induce metabolic changes similar to those seen under hypoxia.

claim: Exosomes themselves might be acting as source of metabolites in a manner similar to macropinocytosis.
source: These results suggested that exosomes themselves might be acting as source of metabolites in a manner similar to macropinocytosis observed recently in Kras expressing pancreatic cancer cells (Commisso et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the inability to fully account for palmitate synthesis from glucose and glutamine alone, and the presence of metabolites in exosomes.

claim: CDEs reprogram cancer cell metabolism through disabling mitochondrial oxidative metabolism and providing de novo 'off the shelf' metabolites through exosomal cargo.
source: Our results demonstrate that patient-derived CDEs reprogram cancer cell metabolism through disabling mitochondrial oxidative metabolism and providing de novo 'off the shelf' metabolites through exosomal cargo.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript showing both mitochondrial inhibition and metabolite supply.

claim: The metabolite cargo delivery mechanism by exosomes is similar to macropinocytosis, albeit without the previously described dependence on oncogenic Kras signaling.
source: Notably, we demonstrate in wild-type and activated Kras-expressing pancreatic cancer cells that the metabolite cargo delivery mechanism by exosomes is similar to macropinocytosis, albeit without the previously described dependence on oncogenic Kras signaling (Commisso et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments comparing wild-type and activated Kras cells and by use of macropinocytosis inhibitors.
